author: Andre Brooks
title: The Lot Next Door Is Knee-Deep in Dry Grass Up to Your Fence, and You Figure It's Yours to Cut. California Stops Your Clearing at the Line. - NewsBreak
text:
8 hours ago Stand at the back fence and look over it at the lot next door: knee-high grass gone gold, dead brush leaning on the boards, none of it cut since spring. On your side, a mown strip and the corner of the house.
Most people read that one of two ways: their lot, so nothing can be done, or your fire risk, so you will end up cutting their side. California's defensible space law answers both.
The job that is yours sits on your side of the fence: checking and clearing the first five feet around your own walls, and pricing that with a local pro.
Home Services › Landscaping & Lawn Care Is the lot next door overgrown? Check my house › Free · Your number stays private What actually happens Public Resources Code section 4291, in the version amended by AB 1455 and effective October 13, 2025, requires owners of buildings in the state responsibility area to keep 100 feet of defensible space around them, "but not beyond the property line." Government Code section 51182 uses the same words for very high fire hazard severity zones that cities and counties designate.
Two more lines in section 4291 settle the fence. Nobody is required to enter or alter property owned by someone else without the owner's consent. And fuel modification on adjacent property may only be done with the adjacent landowner's written consent. The Board of Forestry and Fire Protection's September 2026 guidance says it in one sentence: California law only requires property owners to manage fuels on their own property.
So your clearing stops at your line. The grass on the far side is not yours to cut, and the state rule does not ask you to.
If there is a house next door, its owner carries the same duty around that house, to their own line. The statute also lets a local ordinance require clearing past a property line to hold 100 feet around a structure, and lets that ordinance split the cost. Kern County's Fire Hazard Reduction Program is one version: the owner of a vacant parcel keeps a fuel break at least 10 feet wide, grass and shrubs removed, along any property line within 100 feet of a neighbor's structure.
Reporting is local too. The City of San Diego's Fire-Rescue Department takes brush and weed complaints about privately owned land inside the city, and says every complaint is investigated. It sends complaints in CAL FIRE's state responsibility area to CAL FIRE. In Kern County, weed complaints go to Code Compliance, which refers those in outlying areas to the fire department. CAL FIRE's defensible space page points residents to their local fire department or fire protection district.
What it is worth No agency page I read prices a neighbor's overgrown lot or says what an insurer does about one. The statute says this much: an insurer may require more than 100 feet only on findings from a designated fire expert, and that distance may not go past the property line unless state law or a local ordinance allows it. The ground you control is your own side.
What to look at on your house Measure from your wall to the property line. Under 100 feet, everything in between is yours; the grass line is not the boundary. Look at the first five feet on your side. Grass that has crept under the fence onto your side is on your side. Write down what you see from your yard. How tall, how dry, how close to your wall. Stay off the lot. Find out who answers for that address. A city fire department, county fire, code compliance, or CAL FIRE. San Diego's page says to contact the jurisdiction the address sits in.
